full_cite: Hollins 26 (Invented Author, Fictional Review of Local Services, 2026)
evidence_text: Municipal composting programmes rarely fail for want of residents willing to sort their waste; they fail because collection schedules are designed around the old landfill contracts. The Hollins review of twenty-two towns found that where food waste was collected weekly, participation held above sixty percent for three years, while towns that collected it fortnightly saw participation fall by half within a year. Residents in the fortnightly towns reported odour and pests as their reasons for stopping, not inconvenience. The review's authors concluded that the cost of a weekly round is recovered within four years through lower landfill charges, and that councils which economise on collection frequency end up paying twice: once for the bins that sit unused, and again for the tipping fees they were meant to avoid.
